analysis.one_liner: Bars injury and property lawsuits against makers of work equipment more than 18 years after sale.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the House Judiciary Committee and received no vote before Congress ended in early 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set a nationwide 18-year cutoff on lawsuits over workplace equipment — anything from factory machines to farm tools — for injury, death, and property damage claims. Once 18 years passed from delivery of the product, an injured worker (except in toxic-exposure cases like asbestos) could no longer sue the maker or seller, even if state law allowed it. The federal rule would have overridden longer state deadlines.
analysis.who_benefits: Manufacturers and sellers of long-lasting work equipment. They would gain certainty that no lawsuit over a machine sold decades ago could reach them, cutting off aging-product liability and the insurance and litigation costs that come with it.

how_it_helps.text: The bill bars civil actions against a durable good's manufacturer or seller for property damage, death, or personal injury if the accident occurs more than 18 years after the product was first delivered to a purchaser or lessee [S2][S3].

Injury claims are cut off only where the claimant received or was eligible for workers' compensation and the harm is not a toxic injury such as asbestos, so manufacturers no longer face suits from workers covered by comp [S2][S3].
The rule preempts and supersedes state laws, imposing the 18-year limit nationwide even where state law would have given claimants more time or no limit at all [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Injured workers and the families of workers killed by old equipment. After 18 years, they would lose the right to sue the manufacturer, and workers' compensation — often far less than a court award — would be the only recovery. Anyone with a pending lawsuit would have had just one year to finish it.

drawbacks.text: The bill would eliminate the right to sue for workers injured or killed by defective equipment simply because the machine was more than 18 years old, leaving workers' compensation as the only recovery even where a defective product caused the harm [S2][S3].
It overrides state law: states that set no repose period or a longer one would have their rules preempted for the lawsuits the bill covers [S3].
Applying the cutoff to accidents occurring after enactment, and giving existing claimants only one year to file, would have extinguished many legitimate claims the moment the bill took effect [S3].

An honest supporter would acknowledge the trade-off: some genuinely defective old machines do injure workers, and evidence for or against old claims can be hard to find — the bill resolves that uncertainty in the manufacturer's favor [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits go to manufacturers, who get a hard 18-year shield from product lawsuits. The costs fall on a narrow but real group: workers hurt by old, defective equipment, who would be left with workers' compensation — typically a fraction of what a court award provides — as their only remedy. Because the injury claims barred by the bill are by definition those where the worker already receives or qualifies for workers' comp, the bill targets the small gap between comp benefits and full legal accountability, and closes it in the manufacturer's favor.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Chabot introduced the bill on March 17, 2005, joined by Rep. Henry Hyde [S1][S3].
It was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary that same day, which was its only action before the Congress ended [S1][S5].
The bill never received a committee vote, a floor vote, or any further action [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers and sellers of durable work equipment, who kept facing product liability exposure under existing state law and avoided a new federal cutoff on old-injury lawsuits.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Equipment manufacturers, who faced no new liability cutoff

for.name: Rep. Steve Chabot
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill establishing an 18-year statute of repose for lawsuits over durable goods used in business.

for.name: Rep. Henry Hyde
for.role: Original cosponsor; former Judiciary Committee chairman
for.what_they_did: Joined Chabot in introducing the bill.

for.name: 4 of 5 cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; of its five cosponsors, four were Republicans and one was a Democrat.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Rep. James Sensenbrenner (R-WI)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress, never scheduling a markup or vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll calls show the split; its five cosponsors were four Republicans and one Democrat, suggesting at least nominal bipartisan sponsorship [S4].

industries.industry: Durable goods manufacturers and sellers (workplace equipment)
industries.note: The bill would have barred most injury and property lawsuits over their products 18 years after sale, cutting off claims from workers hurt by old, defective machines. Their gain is precisely the loss of those workers' remedy.

Where a lawsuit is barred, workers' compensation becomes the sole recovery, which shifts claims toward and slightly increases reliance on the comp system. Comp benefits are generally lower than tort awards, so workers' net recovery falls.
Lawyers who represent injured workers in product suits would lose the contingent-fee cases the bill bars, an interest that runs alongside their clients' loss of recovery.
